subject: physics
title: X-ray imaging and CT scanning
key_idea: X-rays are made when fast electrons hit a metal target. Tissues absorb them by different amounts, so the transmitted beam forms a shadow image, with intensity falling as I = I₀e^(−μx). A CT scanner combines many X-ray images from different angles into slices and then a 3D image.

blocks.text: X-rays are produced when electrons that have been accelerated by a high voltage hit a metal target. Most of the electrons' energy becomes heat, and only a small fraction becomes X-rays.

items: A **heated cathode** (filament) releases electrons by thermionic emission.
A high p.d. of tens of kilovolts between the cathode and the **anode** accelerates the electrons across a vacuum.
The electrons hit a **target** metal embedded in the anode, such as tungsten, which has a high melting point.
The anode rotates, so the beam hits a fresh part of the target and the heat is spread over a larger area.

items.text: Electrons are decelerated as they enter the target. They lose different amounts of energy, so they produce photons of all energies up to a maximum.
The most energetic photon comes from an electron that loses all its kinetic energy in one go. Its energy is eV, so it has the minimum wavelength.
An electron can knock out an inner electron from an atom of the target. An outer electron drops into the gap and emits a photon of a fixed energy, which makes a sharp line in the spectrum.

rows: Intensity of the beam
The heater current
A hotter filament emits more electrons, so more X-ray photons are made each second.
Photon energy (penetration)
The tube voltage
A larger p.d. gives the electrons more energy, so the photons have more energy.
Sharpness of the image
A small area of target and a narrow beam
A small source casts a sharp shadow with less blurring at the edges.
Patient dose
A metal filter, a short exposure and a narrow beam
A filter, such as aluminium, removes low-energy photons that would be absorbed by the patient and not help to form the image.
Contrast
A lower tube voltage and a lead grid
Lower-energy photons are absorbed more differently by different tissues. A lead grid absorbs scattered photons, which would blur the image.

items: X-rays come from electrons hitting a metal target. The spectrum has a continuous part and sharp characteristic lines.
The maximum photon energy is eV, which sets the minimum wavelength.
Heater current sets the intensity. Tube voltage sets the photon energy.

blocks.text: As X-rays pass through the body, some photons are absorbed or scattered. The transmitted beam is weaker, and by different amounts for different tissues.

items: Each equal layer of material removes the same **fraction** of the intensity. This is an exponential decrease.
μ depends on the material and on the photon energy. Bone has a larger μ than soft tissue, because it is denser and contains atoms with a larger atomic number.
Different tissues absorb different amounts, so the transmitted beam forms a shadow image of the structures inside the body.

diagram.alt: A practice question. Work out the percentage of an X-ray beam transmitted through a thickness of tissue.
diagram.question: An X-ray beam passes through {x} cm of tissue with an attenuation coefficient μ = {mu} cm⁻¹. What percentage of the intensity is transmitted?

items.meaning: The difference in the degree of blackening (or brightness) between two structures in an image.
A substance with a high atomic number that absorbs X-rays strongly and is put into soft tissue so that it shows up.

items: Bone shows up clearly against soft tissue, because their attenuation coefficients are very different.
Soft tissues have similar coefficients, so the contrast between them is poor.

A contrast medium is swallowed, injected or inserted to improve this. **Barium** sulphate shows up the digestive system (the barium meal), and **iodine** compounds show up blood vessels and organs such as the kidneys.
These elements have a large atomic number, so they absorb X-rays much more than soft tissue does.
Intensity falls exponentially with thickness: I = I₀e^(−μx).
Differences in μ between tissues make the contrast in an image.
Barium and iodine are contrast media that absorb X-rays strongly.

blocks.text: A computed tomography (CT) scan builds up an image of a slice through the body from many X-ray images. Repeating this along the body gives a 3D image.

items.text: An X-ray tube produces a thin beam, which passes through one slice of the patient.
Detectors on the opposite side measure the intensity of the transmitted beam.
The tube and detectors rotate around the patient, taking images from many different angles.
A computer combines all the images in that slice to calculate a 2D image of the slice.
The patient moves along the axis and the process repeats. The computer stacks the slices into a 3D image.

items: A CT image shows a slice, so structures are not drawn on top of one another as they are in a single X-ray image.
It shows much smaller differences in tissue density, so soft tissue such as the brain and tumours can be seen.
The 3D image can be viewed from any angle and sliced in any direction.
The patient receives a much larger dose of ionising radiation than from a single X-ray image.
CT combines X-ray images from many angles into a slice, and slices into a 3D image.
Compared with a single X-ray image, a CT scan shows more detail in soft tissue but gives a larger dose.

checks.q: Calculate the minimum wavelength of the X-rays produced by a tube operating at 60 kV.
The intensity of an X-ray beam falls to 40% of its original value after passing through 3.0 cm of tissue. Calculate the attenuation coefficient.
Explain why a barium meal is used before an X-ray image of the stomach and why a CT scan shows more detail than a single X-ray image.
checks.a: Soft tissue absorbs X-rays by similar amounts, so the contrast is poor. Barium has a high atomic number and absorbs X-rays strongly, so the stomach shows up. A CT scan combines images from many angles into slices, so structures do not overlap, and it shows small differences in tissue density.

blocks.text: Mass attenuation coefficient and half-value thickness

blocks.label: Mass attenuation coefficient
where: ρ = density of the material (kg m⁻³)

items: The **half-value thickness** is the thickness of material that reduces the intensity to half its initial value.
Putting I = I₀ ÷ 2 into I = I₀e^(−μx) gives half-value thickness = ln 2 ÷ μ.

**Photographic film with an intensifying screen:** the screen is a fluorescent material which gives out many visible photons for each X-ray photon. This darkens the film more, so a shorter exposure and a smaller dose are needed.

**Fluoroscopic image intensifier:** X-rays hit a fluorescent screen and the light releases electrons from a photocathode. The electrons are accelerated and focused onto a small screen, which gives a brighter live image with less dose.

**Flat panel detector:** a scintillator turns each X-ray photon into light, and a photodiode pixel under it turns the light into charge. The pixels are read out by electronic scanning to give a digital image.
The flat panel detector gives an immediate digital image with no chemical processing, can be stored and enhanced by computer, and needs a smaller dose than film.

blocks.text: Contrast is helped by a lower tube voltage and a grid to cut out scattered X-rays. Dose is reduced by filtering out low-energy photons and by intensifying screens.

items: The beam is narrow and **monochromatic**: filtered to one photon energy, so the attenuation depends on the tissue and not on the spectrum.
Compared with a single X-ray image, a CT scan gives a clearer image of soft tissue, but the equipment is much more expensive and the dose is larger.

extra.heading: Detail this course asks for: how X-rays are attenuated

blocks.text: Four processes remove photons from an X-ray beam. Which process dominates depends on the photon energy and on the material.

rows: Simple (coherent) scatter
A low-energy photon changes direction without losing energy. No ionisation happens.
Photoelectric effect
A photon is completely absorbed by an atom and releases an electron. It is much more likely in materials with a large atomic number, such as bone, and for lower photon energies.
Compton effect
A photon collides with an outer electron, releasing it. The photon loses some energy and is scattered in a new direction.
Pair production
A photon with energy of at least 1.02 MeV passes near a nucleus and becomes an electron and a positron.

items: The photoelectric effect is an important process at diagnostic energies, and it is mainly responsible for the contrast between bone and soft tissue.
Pair production is not important for diagnostic X-rays, because the photon energies are far below 1.02 MeV.
A rotating X-ray tube gives a thin, fan-shaped beam.
A ring of detectors surrounds the patient and measures the transmitted intensity.
Computer software combines the signals into an image, which is shown on a display.
